title: Is It Cheating If My Child Uses an AI Tutor for IB?
summary: Learn when AI tutoring is acceptable in the IB, when it becomes academic misconduct, and how parents can help students use AI responsibly.
body_markdown:
If you are asking, **“Is it cheating if my child uses an AI tutor for IB?”** , the short answer is **no, not automatically** . AI can explain concepts, provide practice, ask questions, or give feedback while the student remains responsible for the thinking and final work.


The line is crossed when AI replaces the student’s authorship or provides unauthorized assessment help. Parents should therefore ask **how the tool was used, what kind of task was involved, and who produced the submitted work** .


### What the IB says about AI and academic integrity


The IB does not impose a general ban on artificial intelligence. Its[statement about ChatGPT and artificial intelligence](https://ibo.org/news/news-about-the-ib/statement-from-the-ib-about-chatgpt-and-artificial-intelligence-in-assessment-and-education/) recognizes that AI tools can support education when their use follows academic integrity expectations.


The IB’s[Academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) defines **student academic misconduct** as deliberate or inadvertent behaviour that may give the student or someone else an unfair advantage in assessment. This means careless use can create a problem even when the student did not intend to cheat.


Two principles are especially important:


-


Submitted work must genuinely represent the student’s achievement.


-


AI-generated words, ideas, images, graphs, calculations, or code are not automatically the student’s own work.


If permitted AI-generated material is included in assessed work, it must be clearly identified and referenced according to the school’s procedures. However, citation does not make every use acceptable. As the IB’s[questions and concerns about AI tools](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/artificial-intelligence-questions-and-concerns-en.pdf) indicate, AI should support learning rather than produce the work for the student.


### AI tutor or AI ghostwriter?


An AI tutor helps a student become capable of completing a task. An AI ghostwriter completes the intellectual work on the student’s behalf.


Generally safer learning support


Potential academic misconduct


Explaining photosynthesis more simply


Writing a Biology IA analysis


Quizzing the student on historical events


Producing a submission-ready History essay


Creating unassessed practice questions


Answering a live test


Identifying an error in practice calculations


Completing assessed calculations


Explaining an IB command term


Generating the final assessed response


Identifying weaknesses in a draft


Rewriting the draft until AI becomes the author


Suggesting search terms


Inventing sources, quotations, results, or data


A useful test is: “Can my child close the tool and complete a similar task independently?” If the student can explain and reproduce the reasoning, the AI probably acted as a tutor. If they cannot explain the vocabulary, claims, or method, it probably did too much.


### Acceptable use depends on the task


Parents should distinguish between **learning activities** and **assessment activities** . The same AI action may be acceptable during revision but prohibited in assessed work.


### Revision and independent practice


AI use is generally lowest-risk when students are revising taught material. They might request another explanation, generate a quiz, compare methods, or receive feedback on an unsubmitted practice answer.


For example, a Mathematics student could ask why a differentiation method failed, close the explanation, and attempt a new problem independently. The tool supports understanding without supplying assessed work.


### Homework and class assignments


Homework rules vary. Some homework is informal practice, while other work contributes to school assessment or demonstrates independent ability.


Students should check the instructions before using AI. A teacher might permit AI-generated practice questions but prohibit feedback on a written response because independent writing is the skill being assessed.


### IAs, the Extended Essay, TOK, and assessed coursework


Coursework requires particular caution. Research decisions, analysis, evaluation, calculations, conclusions, and final expression must represent the student’s achievement.


AI should not generate final paragraphs, interpret results for the student, manufacture references, create reflections, or substantially rewrite coursework. Changing a few words does not necessarily transfer authorship to the student. RevisionDojo’s[guide to using AI for an IB IA safely](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/is-ai-allowed-in-ib-using-ai-for-your-ia-safely) explains these boundaries in more detail.


### Tests and examinations


Unless AI is expressly authorized, using it during a test or examination is unauthorized assistance, not tutoring. Students must also never use AI to access, reconstruct, share, or discuss protected examination content.


### Citation does not make every use acceptable


Referencing AI provides **transparency** , but it does not prove that the assistance was permitted. An assessment must still demonstrate the student’s own knowledge and skills.


Students should ask two separate questions:


1.


**Must this AI contribution be disclosed or cited?**


2.


**Was this type of assistance allowed at all?**


A citation cannot make an AI-written evaluation or essay acceptable if the student was expected to perform that work independently. Because procedures differ, students should consult the subject teacher or IB coordinator before incorporating generated material into an assessment.


### School rules may be stricter


The IB provides the overall framework, but individual IB World Schools establish local procedures. A school may restrict particular tools, require an AI-use declaration, specify how prompts are recorded, or prohibit AI during certain coursework stages.


Parents and students should ask:


-


Which tools and uses are permitted?


-


Is AI allowed for planning, feedback, or editing?


-


How should prompts and outputs be documented?


-


When must AI use be acknowledged?


-


Are there subject-specific restrictions?


-


May schoolwork be uploaded to third-party platforms?


Families should also review a tool’s age requirements and privacy practices before uploading personal information, drafts, research, or school documents.


### A practical framework for parents


A simple **explain, close, apply** routine preserves independent thinking:


1.


**Explain:** Use AI to clarify one specific difficulty.


2.


**Close:** Hide the generated response.


3.


**Apply:** Complete a fresh task independently.


For coursework, students should retain outlines, source records, calculations, earlier drafts, teacher feedback, and version history. A basic AI log can record the date, tool, prompt, purpose, information verified, and work completed independently.


Parents can then ask process-focused questions: “What did the AI help you understand?”, “Can you explain this without looking?”, and “Did your teacher permit that assistance?” RevisionDojo’s[parent guide to supporting IB academic integrity](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/the-role-of-parents-in-supporting-ib-academic-integrity) provides further guidance without encouraging parents to take over the work.


### Using Jojo AI responsibly


Jojo AI can function as a tutor when prompts develop understanding rather than generate submissions. Suitable prompts include:


-


“Explain this concept using a simpler example.”


-


“Quiz me one question at a time.”


-


“Give me one hint, but not the answer.”


-


“Identify the incorrect step in my practice calculation.”


-


“Ask questions that test my argument.”


-


“Explain what the command term ‘evaluate’ requires.”


Students should then produce their own response and verify important claims. RevisionDojo’s[AI ethics guide for IB coursework](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-ai-tools-can-be-used-ethically-in-ib-coursework-based-on-ib-guidelines) and[guide to avoiding plagiarism and collusion](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-academic-misconduct-explained-how-to-avoid-plagiarism-and-collusion) provide additional checks.


### Warning signs that AI is doing too much


Concern is appropriate when a student cannot explain their submission, accepts references without opening them, has no drafts or visible development process, hides AI use, or produces work far beyond their established voice. Pasting an assessment prompt into AI before attempting it is another warning sign.


These signs do not prove cheating, but they justify pausing before submission and consulting the teacher. RevisionDojo’s[guide to IB academic misconduct penalties](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-the-penalties-for-academic-misconduct-in-ib-full-guide-for-students-and-parents) explains why early clarification is safer than addressing a concern afterward.


### Conclusion


Using an AI tutor for IB is not inherently cheating. It becomes academically dishonest when AI provides unauthorized assistance, replaces the student’s thinking or authorship, or is used without required transparency.


Parents can protect learning by checking school rules, separating revision from assessment, preserving evidence of process, and asking students to demonstrate understanding independently. RevisionDojo’s Jojo AI, Questionbank, Flashcards, Study Notes, and Mock Exams are most useful when they support practice without producing assessed work for the student.
